title: The royal way of the cross (II.12)
word: The royal way of the cross
hookLine: the cross is everywhere; carry it and it carries you
tomorrow: what if the voice you need is quieter than every notification?

cards: Can carrying something heavy make it lighter? A backpack hanging off one shoulder drags all day. Cinch both straps, pull it in close, and the same weight rides easier.

Nothing in the bag changed; the carrying did. Chapter twelve of book two makes a claim like that about the cross. It admits that deny yourself, take up your cross and follow sounds like a hard saying to many.
Then it calls the road royal: the king's highway.

teach.b: Ask the Imitation how to carry what can't be put down, and it answers: willingly. In the cross is salvation, the chapter says, in the cross is life, protection, strength of mind, joy of spirit.

In the Latin it begins, in cruce salus. And the king walks the road first: he went ahead, the book says, carrying his own cross. You can't outrun it, either, because wherever you go, you bring yourself along.

teach.h: CARRY IT, AND IT CARRIES YOU.
teach.b: Carry the cross willingly and it will carry you, and lead you where you long to go. Carry it unwillingly and you make it heavier, and you still have to carry it. That's the backpack.
Same weight, different carrying. A neighbor tradition says something close about burdens.
In the Qur'an, Pickthall's translation reads: "Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope." Both refuse to treat a burden as pointless, and both face it with God rather than alone.
And here's one honest difference worth naming.
The Imitation asks the reader to take up the cross, even to love it, because Christ carried his first. That same Qur'an verse closes with a prayer asking God not to lay on us more than we can bear.
One posture picks the weight up and walks behind the king; the other trusts the measure and asks for mercy in it. Each in its own words.

how: Catholics pray the Stations of the Cross, especially in Lent, walking with Jesus from his condemnation to the tomb, and many speak of uniting their own sufferings with his.

games.q: what does “the royal way of the cross” mean?
o: a hunt for suffering to prove your faith
a pilgrimage road reserved for royalty
the cross carried willingly, as Jesus did first

games.q: the king's road, and a neighbor — tap the pairs.
p: no soul tasked beyond its scope

s: the way of the cross means going looking for suffering
the chapter is about the burden already yours, picked up willingly instead of dragged.
the Qur'an says God tasks no soul beyond its scope
Pickthall: "Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope" (2:286).
the Imitation and the Qur'an teach the same thing about the cross
both face burdens with God; the cross at the center is the Imitation's, and the verse asks for mercy in the load.

games.q: your mom works a double shift and still has dinner to make; she can't skip it. by chapter twelve, what can change the load?
o: how it's carried: taken up willingly, it gets lighter.
figuring out exactly who's to blame for the double.
finding some way to make the work disappear.
games.why: carry the cross willingly, the chapter says, and it carries you; drag it, and it gets heavier and still has to be carried.

practice: Pick up something with a little weight, a book or a bag, and hold it close against you with both arms. Breathe out the complaint and keep the weight; no need to lift much, and notice how it rides when it's held instead of dragged.
If you pray, ask for the grace to carry yours willingly.

wordCard.voice: The royal way of the cross. The Imitation's name for the road Jesus walked first: the cross carried willingly, as a king's highway.

orig.note: Latin, from the title of the Imitation II.12: the royal way, the king's road of the holy cross.

carryVoice: Your line: carry it, it carries you, like a backpack pulled in close and held. Peace to you.
